problem: RL image-goal navigation policies predict single-step actions and are myopic; generative (diffusion / flow-matching) navigation policies need iterative sampling (high latency) and rely on imitation only, while distilling them to one step degrades trajectory quality.
motivation: Real-time deployment on resource-constrained robots needs fast trajectory generation, and imitation alone cannot fix suboptimal expert behavior or align generation with task objectives such as goal reaching and collision avoidance. MeanFlow's average-velocity modeling allows one-step generation without distillation, and RL can then align the generator with task rewards.
key_idea: Use a MeanFlow average-velocity generator for one-step trajectory synthesis in image-goal navigation, pretrain it with imitation plus a safety-aware trajectory evaluator, then refine it with PPO by injecting learnable noise to make the transport chain stochastic.
insight: Both training stages matter: without the IL stage SR collapses to 13.2 on Gibson (versus 68.7 full), and without RL SR is 51.3, so RL contributes a large gain in SR, SPL and collision rate. The evaluator adds a further gain over random candidate selection (SR 60.7 to 68.7), mainly through fewer collisions. One-step MeanFlow reaches about 19.6 ms versus 47-90 ms for multi-step baselines and beats distilled baselines, which lose accuracy.
method: Observation encoding: two EfficientNet-B0 backbones for RGB and depth, plus a third EfficientNet-B0 on the concatenated current and goal RGB; features are fused by a Transformer into a latent C_t
MeanFlow generator: a UNet conditioned on C_t via FiLM predicts the average velocity u(x,r,t) from Gaussian noise, producing a waypoint trajectory in one step; trained with a MeanFlow regression loss

Trajectory evaluator: an MLP scores candidate trajectories, regressing a target built from obstacle-distance-field clearance (barrier penalty, clearance progress) minus a smoothness penalty; the top-scored candidate is executed

Stochastic transport for RL: a learnable noise head gives Gaussian transitions, so the trajectory log-likelihood factorizes over transport steps; at inference it collapses to a deterministic τ = X + U(X,Z)
Online PPO refinement: Transformer and evaluator frozen, generator and noise head fine-tuned in Habitat with reward = success (5) + slack (-0.01) + progress + collision (-0.1)
Data and control: Hybrid A* expert trajectories in Gibson/MP3D plus GoStanford and SCAND (depth from Depth Anything V2); a topological graph gives sub-goals and a PD controller tracks the waypoints

setting.backbone: EfficientNet-B0 encoders + Transformer + MeanFlow UNet + MLP evaluator (trained from scratch, IL then PPO)
setting.training_data: Hybrid A* expert trajectories on the Gibson training split (MP3D used for zero-shot generalization), plus real-world GoStanford and SCAND episodes; then online RL in Habitat
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + depth + goal RGB image, with a pre-built topological graph
setting.action_space: predicted waypoint trajectories tracked by a PD controller into continuous velocities (v, ω)
setting.privileged: pre-built topological graph of the environment; obstacle distance field used for evaluator supervision during training only

numbers.extra: topological graph provided; success = within 1.0 m and 30°; trained on Gibson train split; text also calls this the validation split
numbers.evidence: Table 1 comparison on Gibson and MP3D, RoamFlow row (unseen Gibson test scenes)

numbers_note: Real-robot results (Unitree Go2, 20 runs per method): RoamFlow SR 1.00, C/run 0.10, time 37.2 ms. These are not listed above because they are not on a canonical benchmark.
results: On Gibson, RoamFlow reaches SR 68.7 / SPL 61.9 / CR 10.9 at 19.6 ms, versus the strongest baseline NavDP at 59.3 / 47.5 / 11.6 and 61.1 ms. On MP3D (no finetuning) it reaches SR 56.1 / SPL 47.1 versus NavDP's 48.1 / 34.1. On the real robot it succeeded in 20/20 runs (SR 1.00), versus 0.90 for FlowNav.
limitations: Evaluated only with a pre-built topological graph and PD controller, so it is not end-to-end mapless; the baselines were adapted to this setup
Real-robot evaluation is small (20 runs over 3 scenarios), with no variance or statistical reporting
Baselines are reimplemented under a custom protocol rather than on a standard benchmark, and the RL stage adds 30 h of training in simulation
